title: Prayer and action

segments.voice: Yesterday, asking and accepting: the Ardas, then the hukam, hands lifted and then left open. Your line was ask, then accept. What did you ask for, and what answer did you receive? Day one thousand four hundred eight.

Before a long drive, before an exam, before a shop opens its doors for the first time, a Sikh family may stand together for an Ardas. Then somebody picks up the car keys. The prayer doesn't replace the driving. Nobody expects the car to steer itself because the prayer was heartfelt. Prayer, then the work. Guru Arjan has a line that holds both halves of that scene in a single breath, and two old friends in the Granth argue it out. Today: prayer and action.
screen: `AN ARDAS BEFORE THE DRIVE.` → `THEN, THE CAR KEYS.` → `BOTH HALVES.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In Gujri ki Var, Guru Arjan writes, in paraphrase: make the effort, and you live; earning, enjoy peace; meditating, meet the Lord; Nanak, the worry is gone. Udam karediaa jeeo toon. Effort, earning, meditation, all in one verse, and none of them cancels the others. Second, two friends. Among the saloks near the end of the Granth is a short exchange between two saints. In paraphrase: Trilochan says, my friend Namdev, you're caught up in the world; why are you busy printing cloth, instead of fixing your mind on the Lord? And Namdev answers: with your mouth, take the Lord's name; with hands and feet, do all your work; keep your mind with the Pure One. Namdev doesn't put the cloth down. The prayer rides along inside the work. Third, the short phrases. Sikhs sum up the life simply: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn by honest work; vand chhako, share what you have. Prayer, work and sharing, braided, the way Namdev's mouth and hands kept moving together. Fourth, the order. Prayer comes first so the work comes from somewhere: humble, honest, aimed at the good of all. Then the work comes, so the prayer goes somewhere. A prayer for a hungry neighbor ends at the stove, with a pot on the flame and a knock on their door. Pray, then do.
screen: `EFFORT, EARNING, MEDITATION.` · `NAMDEV AT HIS CLOTH.` · `NAAM, KIRAT, VAND.` · `PRAYER FIRST, THEN THE STOVE.` · then, large: `PRAY, THEN DO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray, then do. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one task waiting for you today, the one you keep circling. For the first part of the sit, simply be still with it. If you pray, you can offer it to God in your own words. If you don't, set an intention for how you want to do it: honestly, carefully, kindly. Then, for the last few breaths, picture the very first physical step: opening the laptop, picking up the phone, putting on your shoes. When the bell rings, you can take that step. The bell holds the time.
Prayer and action. In the Sikh pattern, prayer gives the work a source, and work gives the prayer somewhere to go. Today's word.
Your line: pray, then do. Today, after one quiet moment, take the very first step of the thing you've been putting off, before the moment fades. Day one thousand four hundred eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs often offer an Ardas before a journey, an exam or a new venture and then set to work; the life is summed up as naam japo (remember the Name), kirat karo (earn honestly) and vand chhako (share).

original.note: Gurmukhi: honest work, earning by one's own labor, as in kirat karo.

trapdoor: what you thought: prayer is what you do instead of acting.
what it means: Sikhs pray first so the work has a source, then act so the prayer has a destination.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan's verse in Gujri ki Var sets effort, earning and meditation side by side.
